messages.content: I want to develop video-language grounding that distinguishes repeated actions through temporal relationships while remaining robust to irrelevant visual changes.

The goal has two parts. The grounding should identify which occurrence of a repeated action a query refers to by using temporal relationships, rather than treating similar-looking occurrences as interchangeable. It should also remain reliable when the background changes but the actions and their timing stay the same.
How should I state the target for distinguishing the occurrences?

Ground both queries correctly in 80% of event-order minimal pairs, with temporal IoU of at least 0.5. The unit in that target is the pair: both queries in a pair need correct grounding for the pair to count.
So getting one query right in a pair is not enough?

Right. “Both queries correctly in 80% of event-order minimal pairs” is stronger than saying that 80% of individual queries are correct. A pair with only one correctly grounded query would not satisfy the both-queries condition.
And what does the temporal IoU threshold contribute?

Temporal intersection over union measures how much a predicted time interval overlaps the intended interval relative to their combined span. The stated threshold is temporal IoU ≥0.5. It makes the grounding requirement about locating the relevant time intervals, not merely recognizing that the queried actions occur somewhere in the video.
Is the main issue that an action can appear more than once?

Yes. When an action repeats, recognizing its visual appearance alone may not distinguish the occurrence a query seeks. The goal calls for distinguishing those occurrences through their temporal relationships. It does not specify a particular model or method for doing so.
Can you explain “event-order minimal pairs” without assuming a particular set of events?

They are pairs that test whether grounding is sensitive to event order. In this goal, the important requirement is that the system ground both queries correctly for at least 80% of those pairs, using temporal IoU ≥0.5 as the grounding threshold. No particular events or query wording are specified.
I also want the visual-robustness requirement to be explicit.

Limit the accuracy loss to 5 percentage points under background changes that preserve the actions and their timing. That condition matters: the background changes, while the action content and when it happens remain unchanged.
Why say percentage points rather than percent?

Percentage points describe an absolute difference between accuracy values. For a purely illustrative calculation, a change from 90% accuracy to 85% accuracy is a loss of 5 percentage points. Those numbers are not reported results; they just clarify the unit used in the requirement.
Does the robustness target specify an absolute accuracy under changed backgrounds?

No. It specifies a limit on the loss—5 percentage points—under background changes that preserve actions and timing. It does not give a separate absolute accuracy target for those changed-background cases.
How do the two requirements fit together?

The event-order target asks whether the grounding distinguishes repeated actions by their temporal relationships: both queries must be grounded correctly in 80% of minimal pairs at temporal IoU ≥0.5. The robustness target asks that changing the background, without changing actions or timing, cost no more than 5 percentage points of accuracy. Together they describe accurate temporal discrimination that is not overly sensitive to irrelevant visual changes.
Would a system meet the goal if it found repeated actions but consistently chose the wrong occurrence?

No. Merely finding an instance of the action does not address the need to distinguish repeated occurrences through temporal relationships. For the event-order minimal-pair target, both queries must receive correct temporal groundings at the stated IoU threshold.
What if it handled event order well but its accuracy dropped sharply when the background changed?

That would address one part of the goal but not the other if the loss exceeded 5 percentage points under changes that preserve the actions and timing. The robustness condition is a separate requirement, not an optional consequence of good event-order grounding.
Likewise, background stability alone would not establish that it understands which repeated occurrence is meant?

Correct. Stable accuracy under background changes does not by itself establish that both queries in event-order minimal pairs are grounded correctly. The temporal-discrimination requirement still has to be satisfied.
I want to avoid implying that these targets have already been achieved.

They should be phrased as development goals or success criteria, not results. For example: develop video-language grounding that distinguishes repeated actions through temporal relationships, with a target of correctly grounding both queries in 80% of event-order minimal pairs at temporal IoU ≥0.5, while limiting accuracy loss to 5 percentage points under background changes that preserve actions and timing.
Is there anything else implicit in the background-change condition?

It confines that robustness requirement to changes that leave the actions and their timing intact. The stated goal does not claim the same loss limit when the actions or their timing change; those would be different conditions.
And the 80% applies to pairs, not to each of the two query types separately?
As written, it applies to event-order minimal pairs for which both queries are grounded correctly. It does not state separate 80% targets for each query considered on its own.
For that goal, I propose training OrderBind with contrastive learning on order-swapped queries over event-instance spans, together with background-swap consistency for robust localization.

That frames OrderBind as a proposed way to address both parts of the goal. The order-swapped queries focus training on distinguishing event instances by their temporal relationships. Background-swap consistency focuses on keeping localization stable when the background changes without changing the actions or their timing. This is a training proposal, not a claim that the targets have been met.
What is the point of making the queries order-swapped?

Swapping the order expressed by a query makes the temporal relationship consequential. If similar actions recur, the grounding should follow which event instance the query identifies through that relationship, rather than settling on a matching-looking occurrence regardless of order.
And “event-instance spans” means we care about the individual occurrences in time?

Yes. The phrase points to the temporal spans of particular event occurrences. That distinction matters when an action repeats: two occurrences may be similar as actions, but they are not interchangeable as localized instances.
How does contrastive learning fit the proposal?

At the conceptual level, contrastive learning is the proposed training approach for making the distinctions expressed by order-swapped queries matter to localization over event-instance spans. The proposal does not specify an exact contrastive loss, how examples are selected, or a model architecture.
So I shouldn't describe a particular negative-sampling recipe as though it's already part of OrderBind?

Right. Nothing here fixes such a recipe. You can say the training is contrastive and uses order-swapped queries over event-instance spans; choosing specific examples, sampling rules, or loss details would add implementation decisions that the proposal has not made.
What does the background-swap consistency part ask for?

It asks for consistency in localization when the background is swapped while the actions and their timing are preserved. The intended distinction is between visual context that changes and the event-instance timing that remains relevant to the query.
Does that mean the background is irrelevant in every possible video-language grounding task?

No. The proposal is narrower. It addresses robustness to background swaps that preserve the actions and their timing; it does not assert that background information is universally irrelevant or that arbitrary visual changes should leave every grounding unchanged.
Could I explain the two training ideas as serving different failure modes?

As a conceptual explanation, yes: order-swapped queries target confusion between repeated event instances, while background-swap consistency targets sensitivity to changed backgrounds during localization. That describes the intended roles of the proposed components, not an observed diagnosis or a measured result.
Is the contrastive component about query wording alone?

Not as stated. The proposal is contrastive learning on order-swapped queries *over event-instance spans*. Its point is the relationship between what the query specifies and where the corresponding event instance falls in time, rather than a contrast between word strings in isolation.
If the action and timing stay fixed through a background swap, what should remain stable?

The relevant localization should remain consistent. The proposal does not prescribe an exact numerical tolerance or a particular consistency loss; it identifies background-swap consistency as a training principle for robust localization.
How should I connect this proposal to the targets we discussed without claiming success?

You can say OrderBind is proposed to pursue the event-order minimal-pair target—both queries grounded correctly in 80% of pairs at temporal IoU ≥0.5—and the robustness target—no more than a 5-percentage-point accuracy loss under background changes preserving actions and timing. Those remain targets; the proposal alone provides no outcome for either one.
Does order-swapping mean the underlying video must be changed?

No such video change is specified. “Order-swapped” describes the queries in this proposal. The separate background-swap component concerns changes to the background while actions and timing are preserved. Beyond those descriptions, the proposal does not lay out how training examples are constructed.
I want a concise description that keeps both components visible.

Propose training OrderBind with contrastive learning on order-swapped queries over event-instance spans to distinguish repeated actions by temporal relationship, alongside background-swap consistency to support robust localization when backgrounds change but actions and timing do not.
Does that sentence imply a particular way of combining the components during training?
No. “Alongside” says both are in the proposal without specifying their scheduling, weighting, or precise training objective. Those details are not established here.
And it doesn't say OrderBind already localizes correctly under swapped backgrounds?

Correct. It states what OrderBind is proposed to be trained for. Whether it achieves accurate event-order grounding or limits accuracy loss under background changes would require results that are not part of this proposal.
Does OrderBind’s background-swap consistency collapse temporally distinct instances of the same action into interchangeable grounding targets?

That is a potential concern, not an established outcome. Background-swap consistency is intended to keep localization stable when the background changes but the actions and their timing do not. It should not imply that two occurrences of the same action at different times are interchangeable. The proposal alone does not tell us whether training will preserve that distinction.
What exactly has to stay the same across a background swap?

The grounding of the event instance identified by the query should stay consistent, because the actions and their timing are preserved. Consistency across backgrounds is different from treating every span containing the same action as the same grounding target.
Can you put that distinction more plainly?

There are two different comparisons. One compares the same event instance before and after an irrelevant background change; the desired localization is stable. The other compares separate occurrences of an action at different times; the system still needs to distinguish them when the query’s temporal relationship calls for one rather than the other.
So visual invariance and temporal invariance aren't the same thing?

Exactly. Robustness to a changed background does not require indifference to when an action occurs. OrderBind’s proposed training needs to tolerate the former difference while retaining the latter distinction.
Why might the consistency idea raise a collapse concern at all?

Because a broadly stated push for consistency can sound as though similar-looking or same-action occurrences should receive similar groundings. That would be a problem if it erased which occurrence a temporally specific query refers to. But the stated proposal does not specify that such occurrences are equated; the concern is about a possible interpretation or outcome, not something we can assert has happened.
How does the order-swapped-query part bear on this question?

It is the part of the proposal aimed directly at temporal discrimination. Contrastive learning on order-swapped queries over event-instance spans is meant to make the queried order matter, even when actions repeat. Background-swap consistency is meant to support stable localization under changes that leave the actions and timing intact. The question is whether both aims can be maintained together, not whether one aim replaces the other.
Would it be correct to say the same-action spans must always be pulled together?

No. Sharing an action label does not make two temporally distinct event instances interchangeable grounding targets. If a query identifies one through its temporal relationship, grounding it to the other would lose the distinction the goal requires.
Suppose the grounding stayed stable under a background swap, but it consistently selected the wrong occurrence. Would that answer my concern?

Stability alone would not rule out the concern. A system could be consistently wrong about which repeated occurrence the query identifies. The relevant question is whether localization stays stable across background changes *and* remains correct for the temporally specified event instance.
Conversely, if it distinguishes the occurrences, is background-swap consistency automatic?

No. Distinguishing the occurrences in one visual setting does not by itself establish robustness when the background changes. Temporal discrimination and background robustness are related aims in the proposal, but neither follows automatically from the other.
Is the collapse question asking whether background swaps change the timing?

No. The background-change condition preserves the actions and their timing. The worry is that training for consistency across those changes might nevertheless make OrderBind insufficiently sensitive to differences *between* event instances at different times.
What would 'interchangeable grounding targets' mean here?

It would mean that a query referring to one occurrence could be grounded to another occurrence of the same action without the system preserving the relevant temporal distinction. That would conflict with the intended use of temporal relationships to identify repeated actions.
Does the proposal say how consistency is applied, precisely enough to settle whether that happens?

No. It names background-swap consistency for robust localization but does not specify its exact formulation or how it interacts with the contrastive training. We therefore cannot infer either that collapse occurs or that it is prevented merely from the proposal’s wording.
Can I phrase the desired boundary as 'stable across backgrounds, selective across event instances'?

Yes. That captures the distinction: changing an irrelevant background should not move the grounding away from the queried instance, while changing which instance the temporal query identifies should still matter. It describes the intended behavior, not a verified property of OrderBind.
How does this connect to the numerical goals without pretending we have a result?

The event-order goal is to ground both queries correctly in 80% of minimal pairs at temporal IoU ≥0.5; that makes correctness for distinct instances important. The robustness goal limits accuracy loss to 5 percentage points under background changes preserving actions and timing. Your question asks whether pursuing the second goal through consistency could undermine the first. Neither target, nor their compatibility in a trained OrderBind model, has been established by this question.
So should I answer the question with a definite yes or no?

Not from the information given. A careful answer is: background-swap consistency does not *by definition* make temporally distinct instances interchangeable, and OrderBind’s order-swapped-query training is proposed to preserve their distinction. Whether the combined training actually avoids collapse remains open.

I have a hypothesis about the collapse concern: instance-aligned background-swap positives should maintain ≥0.15 cosine distance between repeated-action spans, versus <0.05 under action-label pairing.

That states a predicted contrast, not an observed result. With background-swap positives aligned to the same event instance, the hypothesis is that temporally distinct spans of a repeated action remain at least 0.15 apart in cosine distance. Under pairing by action label, it predicts a cosine distance below 0.05 between those spans.
Why does aligning positives by instance matter to the question I asked?

The question is whether background-swap consistency makes separate occurrences of the same action interchangeable. Instance alignment treats an occurrence across background changes as the correspondence to preserve. It does not, by itself, identify a different occurrence as the same target merely because the action label matches. Your hypothesis predicts that this distinction will be reflected in the distance between repeated-action spans.
And action-label pairing is the comparison condition?

Yes. The comparison in the hypothesis is with action-label pairing, for which you predict <0.05 cosine distance between repeated-action spans. The contrast is specifically between aligning background-swap positives by event instance and pairing them by action label; it is not a claim about every possible training approach.
Am I saying that the two occurrences have different action labels?

No. They are repeated-action spans, so the point is that they can share an action label while still being distinct event instances in time. The hypothesis asks whether the way positives are paired preserves that instance distinction.
What does 'maintain ≥0.15 cosine distance' convey here?

It conveys a predicted lower bound on the separation between repeated-action spans under instance-aligned background-swap positives: their cosine distance should be at least 0.15. It does not specify that the distance must equal 0.15, nor does it report a measured value.
Is <0.05 also a bound rather than a particular measurement?

Yes. Under action-label pairing, the hypothesis predicts a cosine distance strictly below 0.05. That is a different, smaller-distance regime than ≥0.15, but both figures remain predictions unless measured.
Could you explain the comparison without turning distance into a grounding score?

The distance concerns how separated the repeated-action spans are in the representation being compared. The hypothesis predicts more separation with instance-aligned background-swap positives and less with action-label pairing. Cosine distance is not itself temporal IoU or grounding accuracy, so this prediction should not be described as meeting the localization targets.
Would a larger distance mean OrderBind definitely picks the right span for every query?

No. Separation between spans could be relevant to keeping instances distinguishable, but the stated cosine-distance hypothesis alone does not establish which span OrderBind would ground for a query. It also does not establish the event-order minimal-pair accuracy or robustness targets.
What would the smaller predicted distance suggest, if the hypothesis held?

A distance below 0.05 under action-label pairing would be consistent with the concern that distinct occurrences are represented as more nearly interchangeable. That would be an interpretation of the predicted comparison, not proof that every grounding decision collapses or that any measured collapse has occurred.
So 'should maintain' is important wording?

Yes. It marks the ≥0.15 separation as an expectation. Likewise, the <0.05 figure for action-label pairing is hypothesized, not established. Presenting either number as an experimental finding would change the claim.
Does instance-aligned mean that all spans of the same action should be far apart?

The hypothesis is narrower: it predicts ≥0.15 cosine distance between repeated-action spans under instance-aligned background-swap positives. It does not make a universal claim about every span sharing an action label or about how far apart unrelated events should be.
And the background swap shouldn't be understood as creating a new temporal instance?

Right. In the stated comparison, an instance-aligned positive relates an event instance across a background swap. The temporally distinct repeated-action spans are the ones whose separation is at issue. Keeping those two relationships separate is central to the hypothesis.
Does the comparison require me to specify a loss function or architecture here?

No. The hypothesis names the pairing conditions and the predicted cosine-distance bounds. It does not provide a particular loss formula, architecture, or measurement procedure, and none is needed to state the hypothesis accurately.
How would you state the hypothesis in one sentence, keeping the uncertainty clear?
Instance-aligned background-swap positives are hypothesized to maintain ≥0.15 cosine distance between temporally distinct repeated-action spans, compared with <0.05 under action-label pairing.
That keeps the comparison about instance identity rather than just whether the actions look alike?

Yes. Both conditions concern repeated-action spans. The predicted difference is associated with whether background-swap positives are aligned to the same event instance or paired by action label, not with a claim that the actions themselves are different.

To examine the concern about repeated actions becoming interchangeable, I plan to build OrderSwap-500 with paired background edits. Then I’ll compare instance-aligned versus action-label consistency using repeated-span cosine distance and paired grounding accuracy.

That is a plan to examine the concern, not a report of completed work. OrderSwap-500 with paired background edits would provide the setting for the comparison. Repeated-span cosine distance would address whether distinct occurrences remain separated, while paired grounding accuracy would address whether the relevant queries are actually grounded correctly.
What is the comparison at the center of the plan?

The comparison is instance-aligned consistency versus action-label consistency. The question is whether aligning consistency to a particular event instance differs from aligning it by a shared action label when the action occurs more than once.
Why include paired background edits?

They put background changes into the comparison while retaining the focus on which event instance a query identifies. The plan says the edits are paired; it does not specify how they will be made or give a completed set of edited examples.
Should I call OrderSwap-500 an existing evaluation set?

No. The stated action is to *build* OrderSwap-500. Calling it an existing, completed set would turn a plan into a result. Its name also does not, by itself, establish details such as its precise composition.
What does repeated-span cosine distance add?

It provides a way to compare the separation of temporally distinct spans containing the repeated action. That bears on whether the spans are being treated as distinct instances. The plan does not specify the exact representation or measurement procedure, so it is best to keep the description at that level.
Why not use that distance alone?

Distance between spans does not by itself say whether a query is grounded to the right one. Paired grounding accuracy adds a task-level measure: it asks whether grounding succeeds for the paired queries, rather than relying only on a measure of span separation.
So the two measures answer related but different questions?

Yes. Repeated-span cosine distance concerns how distinct the occurrences remain in the comparison being measured. Paired grounding accuracy concerns the resulting grounding of queries. Looking at both would make the comparison more informative about the possibility of interchangeability.
Does 'paired grounding accuracy' mean I’ve already chosen a particular scoring threshold for this plan?
Not in this node. The plan names paired grounding accuracy as a measure, but it does not specify a threshold or a full scoring protocol. Those details should not be presented as decisions made here.
Can the plan tell us now whether background-swap consistency causes collapse?
No. It sets up a comparison intended to examine that question. Until OrderSwap-500 is built and the comparison is carried out, the plan supplies neither measured distances nor grounding accuracies.
How should I describe the instance-aligned side without overspecifying it?

Call it the instance-aligned consistency condition: consistency is aligned with a particular event occurrence rather than assigned solely because spans share an action label. The plan does not specify an exact training loss or implementation.
And the action-label side?

Call it the action-label consistency condition. It is the comparison condition organized around a shared action label. The important contrast is that the same action can occur in temporally distinct spans, so sharing the label is not necessarily the same as identifying the queried instance.
Would it be fair to say that one measure checks distinction and the other checks usefulness for grounding?

As a shorthand, yes. Repeated-span cosine distance examines separation between repeated-action spans; paired grounding accuracy examines whether the paired grounding decisions are correct. Neither measure should be described as already showing an advantage for either consistency condition.
Do paired background edits mean the different occurrences get swapped with each other?

No such swap is stated. The plan specifies *background* edits that are paired, not an exchange of temporally distinct action instances. The distinction between those instances is what the comparison is meant to examine.
I want to keep the plan tied to the question rather than imply a broader benchmark claim.

Then frame it narrowly: build OrderSwap-500 with paired background edits and compare instance-aligned against action-label consistency on repeated-span cosine distance and paired grounding accuracy to investigate whether background-swap consistency makes temporally distinct repeated actions interchangeable as grounding targets.
Does that wording claim that either condition will perform better?
No. It states what will be compared and why. It leaves the distances, accuracies, and answer to the collapse question open.
The activity is to train OrderBind with instance-aligned or action-label positives, then evaluate repeated-span cosine distance and paired grounding accuracy on OrderSwap-500 background edits.

That describes two training conditions and two evaluation measures. The training comparison changes how positives are paired: by event instance or by action label. The evaluation then examines both the separation between repeated-action spans and the accuracy of grounding paired queries on the OrderSwap-500 background edits. It does not state the outcome of either condition.
Does “or” mean choosing one condition and dropping the other?

Not in this comparison. It identifies the alternative positive-pairing conditions under which OrderBind is trained. Comparing them requires evaluating the instance-aligned condition and the action-label condition; the activity does not say which will perform better.
What distinction is the positive pairing meant to test?

Instance-aligned positives are tied to a particular occurrence across the relevant background edit. Action-label positives are tied by the action label, which can be shared by occurrences at different times. Comparing those conditions addresses whether preserving instance identity matters when the action repeats.
Is the background edit supposed to change which occurrence a query refers to?

No. The background-change setting preserves the actions and their timing. The issue is whether OrderBind can remain robust to that visual change without treating temporally distinct occurrences of the same action as interchangeable targets.
What does repeated-span cosine distance tell us in this activity?

It evaluates separation between spans of repeated actions. That makes it relevant to the concern about distinct occurrences becoming too similar in the representation being compared. The activity does not specify the exact representation used to calculate the distance or report any distance values.
And why evaluate paired grounding accuracy as well?

Because span separation and correct localization are not the same measurement. Paired grounding accuracy checks grounding performance on the paired queries. A cosine-distance measurement alone would not establish that OrderBind chooses the occurrence identified by each query.
Could one condition have greater span separation without necessarily having better paired grounding accuracy?

Conceptually, yes; the two measures assess different things. The activity calls for evaluating both rather than assuming that one determines the other. It gives no results from which to say whether that happens here.
How does this activity relate to the predicted cosine-distance contrast?

Training under the two positive-pairing conditions and measuring repeated-span cosine distance provides a way to examine that prediction. The hypothesis anticipates ≥0.15 cosine distance with instance-aligned background-swap positives versus <0.05 with action-label pairing. Those bounds remain predictions; this activity supplies no measurements.
Does paired grounding accuracy test the same prediction?

It addresses the related grounding question rather than being another expression of the cosine-distance bounds. It asks whether the paired queries are grounded correctly under the two conditions, which matters because representational separation alone does not settle whether repeated occurrences are interchangeable in grounding.
Should I say the activity proves background-swap consistency is safe if the distances are far apart?

No. The activity is to train and evaluate, and distance is only one of its measures. Any conclusion about grounding would also need to respect the paired grounding accuracy evaluation. No such conclusion is supplied here.
Does this description require a particular architecture for OrderBind?

No. It identifies OrderBind, the two positive-pairing conditions, the OrderSwap-500 background edits, and the two evaluation measures. It does not specify an architecture, loss formula, or training schedule.
Nor does it say exactly how the background edits are generated?
Correct. The activity names OrderSwap-500 background edits as the evaluation setting. It does not give an edit-generation procedure, and none should be inferred from the activity description.
Can you state the activity in one sentence without making it sound like results have already been obtained?

Train OrderBind using either instance-aligned or action-label positives, and evaluate each condition on OrderSwap-500 background edits using repeated-span cosine distance and paired grounding accuracy.
Would it be accurate to describe the two evaluations as looking at instance distinction and query grounding, respectively?

Yes, as a concise description of their roles. Repeated-span cosine distance examines how separated the repeated-action instances remain, while paired grounding accuracy examines whether the paired queries are localized correctly. The activity leaves the values and the comparison between conditions open.

I have the OrderSwap-500 results: repeated-span cosine distance was 0.18 with instance-aligned positives versus 0.04 with action-label positives. Paired accuracy was 83% on clean examples and 80% on background-edited examples.

Those are two distinct findings. The repeated-action spans had a cosine distance of 0.18 in the instance-aligned condition, compared with 0.04 in the action-label condition. The reported paired accuracy was 83% clean and 80% background-edited, an absolute decrease of 3 percentage points.
Can you make the distance comparison easy to read?

The repeated-action spans were farther apart by the reported cosine-distance measure with instance-aligned positives: 0.18 versus 0.04 with action-label positives. The difference between those distances is 0.14.
Does the smaller action-label distance mean its spans are the same event instance?

No. The measurement concerns repeated-action spans, which can be distinct occurrences even when they share an action label. A cosine distance of 0.04 says they were closer by that measure in the action-label condition; it does not change their temporal identity.
What does the 0.18 figure tell us without overstating it?

It is the measured repeated-span cosine distance for the instance-aligned condition on OrderSwap-500. It shows greater separation than the reported 0.04 under action-label pairing. By itself, it does not tell us whether a particular query was grounded to the correct span.
That's why we also have paired accuracy?
Yes. Paired accuracy reports grounding performance rather than the distance between spans. Here it is reported separately for clean and background-edited examples: 83% and 80%, respectively.
How should I describe the clean-to-edited change?

Say that paired accuracy decreased from 83% on clean examples to 80% on background-edited examples, a loss of 3 percentage points. Calling it a 3% relative loss would use a different calculation and would not express the reported difference as directly.
Are the accuracy figures broken out by instance-aligned versus action-label positives?

Not in the evidence as stated. The cosine distances are assigned to the two positive-pairing conditions. The 83% clean and 80% background-edited paired accuracies are reported without a corresponding condition-by-condition breakdown, so I would not assign either accuracy to one pairing condition.
Could I say the action-label condition got 80% on background edits?

No. That would attribute the 80% figure to a specific pairing condition that the reported evidence does not identify. You can state the accuracy by clean versus background-edited setting, and state the cosine distance by positive-pairing condition.
What about saying that 83% was the instance-aligned clean score?
That would have the same problem. The report gives 83% as clean paired accuracy, but it does not explicitly label it as the instance-aligned condition’s clean accuracy.
How do these measurements bear on the worry that repeated actions become interchangeable?

The distance comparison is directly relevant: repeated-action spans were more separated under instance-aligned positives than under action-label positives. The paired-accuracy figures add information about grounding on clean and background-edited examples. Neither number alone demonstrates that every temporally distinct occurrence is treated correctly in every query.
So I shouldn't turn 'more separated' into 'never confused'?

Right. A measured difference in cosine distance does not establish that confusion never occurs. Likewise, paired accuracies of 83% and 80% are aggregate figures, not a guarantee about each individual pair.
Is there any arithmetic comparison besides the 3-point accuracy loss that is useful here?

You can note that the reported cosine distances differ by 0.14: 0.18 minus 0.04. Keep that difference in cosine-distance units, separate from the 3-percentage-point difference between the accuracy figures.
Why keep those differences separate?

They compare different quantities. The 0.14 difference compares separation between repeated-action spans across positive-pairing conditions. The 3-percentage-point difference compares paired accuracy across clean and background-edited examples. One should not be presented as a change in the other.
Does the name OrderSwap-500 tell us how many individual spans contributed to each measurement?
Not from these results alone. The reported evidence names OrderSwap-500 and gives the distances and accuracies, but it does not state the number of spans or pairs behind each figure.
Can I infer a confidence interval or variability from these values?
No. The figures provide point values only. They do not include uncertainty estimates, variation across runs, or a distribution of distances.
Give me a careful results sentence that preserves exactly what was measured.

On OrderSwap-500, repeated-span cosine distance was 0.18 with instance-aligned positives versus 0.04 with action-label positives; reported paired accuracy was 83% on clean examples and 80% on background-edited examples.
And if I add an interpretation?

You can say the reported distance comparison shows greater separation between repeated-action spans under instance-aligned pairing, while the reported paired accuracy is 3 percentage points lower on background-edited than on clean examples. Keep those observations distinct, and avoid assigning the accuracy figures to a positive-pairing condition without a stated breakdown.
I want to use the 0.18-versus-0.04 separation to set a 0.10 collapse cutoff, then measure both OrderBind variants on held-out OrderSwap-500 scene swaps.

That sets up a follow-up measurement. The 0.10 cutoff is in cosine-distance units and lies between the reported repeated-span distances of 0.18 for the instance-aligned variant and 0.04 for the action-label variant. Measuring both variants on held-out OrderSwap-500 scene swaps would show how their repeated-action spans compare against that cutoff in the held-out setting.
Why use a cutoff between those two distances?

It gives the collapse question an operational boundary for the next measurement. A repeated-span cosine distance on the lower side of 0.10 would indicate less separation under this criterion; one on the higher side would indicate more. Choosing the boundary from the 0.18-versus-0.04 contrast does not establish where either variant will fall on held-out scene swaps.
Is 0.10 the midpoint of 0.18 and 0.04?
No. Their midpoint is 0.11. The proposed cutoff is 0.10, which is between the two values but is not their exact midpoint.
I don't want to call the cutoff an accuracy threshold.

You shouldn't. The 0.10 cutoff concerns repeated-span cosine distance—separation between temporally distinct occurrences of a repeated action. Accuracy measures whether queries are grounded correctly and uses a different scale.
Does the cutoff itself tell us whether an instance is grounded correctly?

No. It gives a criterion for interpreting measured span separation as a possible collapse signal. A distance above the cutoff would not, by itself, prove correct grounding, and a distance below it would not identify which query was grounded incorrectly.
What is being held out in this activity?

The activity specifies held-out OrderSwap-500 scene swaps as the setting for measuring both variants. It does not give a split procedure or describe the individual held-out swaps, so those details should remain unstated.
Are the two variants still the instance-aligned and action-label versions of OrderBind?

Yes. “Both variants” refers to those two positive-pairing conditions. The next measurement compares them on the held-out scene swaps rather than assuming that the earlier 0.18 and 0.04 distances will recur there.
Should I say that the action-label variant has already collapsed on the held-out swaps?

No. Its 0.04 distance is part of the contrast used to choose the 0.10 cutoff; this activity has not supplied a measurement for the held-out scene swaps. The purpose of measuring both variants there is to see what happens in that setting.
